title: The Image of God: A Bible Study on Human Worth
subtitle: A five-session study on the imago Dei and the dignity it gives every person.
summary:
This study is for anyone who has wondered what a human being is worth, and why, and who is tired of hearing the answer either puffed up into flattery or shrunk down to chemistry. It moves through five sessions on the oldest and boldest thing the Bible says about people: they're made in the image of God. We start in Genesis 1, with a sentence that sounded closer to sedition than to compliment in the world that first heard it, because the empires around Israel kept the divine image in the palace and Genesis gave it to everyone. Then we look at the three classic accounts of what the image is, and why that argument decides who gets counted as fully human. We face the fall, where the image was defaced but never erased. We follow the doctrine to Christ, who is the image of God, and into whose likeness the broken image is being remade. And we end in the street, with the poor, the unborn, the enemy, the stranger and the person who gets on your nerves, each one carrying a worth you didn't assign and can't revoke.

This isn't a study that admires human dignity from a safe height. Most of us assign worth on a sliding scale, generous to the useful and stingy toward the inconvenient, and I'm no exception. The doctrine of the image won't let you look down on a single human being without looking up into the face of the God who made them, and the people we find easiest to despise turn out to be the ones it was written to protect.
audience: Adults, small groups, and anyone wrestling with human worth and dignity

sessions.title: The Image the Kings Kept for Themselves
sessions.aim: To read Genesis 1:26-27 in the world that first heard it, to see what the word image claimed against the empires around Israel, and to grasp that Genesis took the divine image out of the palace and gave it to everyone, refusing both the flattery that makes it a compliment to human greatness and the reduction that makes a human one more animal.
sessions.summary:
"Then God said, 'Let us make man in our image, after our likeness'" (Genesis 1:26). We hear a warm compliment. In the world it was first spoken into, it was closer to sedition. The civilizations around Israel had their own ways of speaking of a divine image, and they kept it in the palace. In Egypt the Pharaoh could be called the image of the god. In Mesopotamia the king could be called the god's image, his representative on earth. The image was a title of empire: one man carried the divine on his face, and everyone else existed to serve him.

Genesis takes that title out of the palace and gives it to everyone, to the slave and the woman and the infant and the enemy, "male and female" (Genesis 1:27). J. Richard Middleton calls this "the liberating image," and the phrase fits.

The modern reduction says a human is a highly evolved animal and the divine image is a story we tell to flatter ourselves. Part of that is true; we really are made of dust. But the reduction can't explain why we keep living as if people matter beyond measure. The image isn't a compliment we pay ourselves. It's a status God gave every human before any of us had done anything to earn it.

keyScripture.why: "So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them" (Genesis 1:27). Every human being bears the image, not only the king or the strong or the useful, and the woman is named in the same breath.

discussion.q: In the ancient world the king was the one called the god's image, and Genesis gives that title to everyone. What changes about the sentence when you hear it as a challenge to empire rather than a compliment to humanity?
discussion.behind: Put the text back in its own world before anyone applies it. Most people have only heard the image as a nice thing said about humans in general. Help the room feel the shock: it demoted every king and promoted every nobody. Land on that reversal; save the application for later.

discussion.q: The Hebrew word for image, tselem, is used elsewhere for a statue that stands for a god. If every human is God's statue set in the temple of his creation, what is a person for?
discussion.behind: Bring out the calling inside the word. An image in an ancient temple was where you went to see what the god was like. Being the image isn't first a fact about what's inside us but a job: to make the invisible God visible and represent him in the world he made. Don't settle the three views yet; that's next session.

discussion.q: Some say a human being is a clever animal and the divine image is a flattering story. What's true in that account, and where does it fail to explain how we actually live?
discussion.behind: Be fair to the skeptic in the room. Our kinship with the animals is real, and Scripture says we're formed from dust. Grant it fully. But the reduction can't account for why we treat human worth as non-negotiable, or why human cruelty outrages us when a lion killing a gazelle doesn't. Let the gap sit open rather than rushing to close it.

discussion.q: Genesis puts male and female in the image in the same sentence, which the surrounding cultures didn't do. Why does it matter that the image was given to exactly the people the ancient world counted as lesser?
discussion.behind: The image is given across every line the ancient world used to rank people, and it lands first on those the world discounted. That's the seed of later claims about human equality. Begin, gently, to ask who we still quietly rank, because the doctrine names them too.

discussion.q: The image isn't something we achieved; God gave it before we'd done anything. Where have you treated your own worth as an achievement, and how would it change you to receive it as a gift?
discussion.behind: Go first, and name your own treadmill. Most of us live as if our worth is earned by what we produce, which is exhausting and also quietly proud. Let the given, unearned image land as relief.

objections.objection: The image of God is a prescientific way of flattering ourselves. We now know human beings are one more species, produced by the same evolutionary process as everything else, and calling that a divine image is wishful thinking.
objections.response: Scripture grants the continuity first. Genesis says the man was formed "of dust from the ground" (Genesis 2:7), a creature among creatures, and the biology that links us to the animals is no threat to the doctrine. Concede all of it. The reduction fails not in what it affirms but in what it can't explain. The person making the objection still lives as if people have a worth atoms and instincts can't deliver. He's outraged by injustice, grieved by cruelty, sure a child matters more than a stone, and none of that follows from the premise that a human is only a clever animal. The image is the missing explanation, the account that makes sense of the dignity everyone already assumes and nobody can build from the ground up. You don't have to believe it to notice that your own moral life is written in its language.

objections.objection: If the image is a calling to represent God and rule the creation, it sounds like a license to dominate and exploit the planet, which is exactly what has gone wrong.
objections.response: That grief points at a real abuse. The dominion of Genesis 1 has been read as permission to plunder, and that reading has done damage. But look at what the word meant in its own world. A king who was called the god's image wasn't licensed to strip the land; he was answerable for ruling as the god would rule. To bear the image is to answer to the one you image, which is the opposite of a blank check. And the man is put in the garden "to work it and keep it" (Genesis 2:15), where keep is a word for guarding. Dominion in the image isn't ownership. It's stewardship on behalf of a King who called his creation good and will ask what we did with it. The abuse is real, and it's a betrayal of the calling, not the calling itself.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Whose face is hardest for you to see the image of God in, and what does that tell you about the worth you've quietly been assigning to people?
sessions.practice: This week, pick one person you tend to look past or look down on: the clerk, the man asking for change, the relative who wears on you. Before you talk with them, tell yourself plainly that this person is the image of God. Don't announce it. Let the sentence sit under the encounter and notice what it does to how you look and speak. Write down what changed in you when you treated an ordinary person as bearing God's image rather than as part of the scenery of your day.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, the kings of the old world kept your image for themselves, and you gave it to everyone: the slave and the woman and the infant and the stranger, all of them made in your likeness. Forgive us for shrinking that gift back down, treating our own worth as something we earned and other people's as something we grade. Teach us to see your image where we've trained ourselves not to look. Make us what you made us to be, showing the world what you're like. We didn't give ourselves this dignity, and we can't take it from anyone else. Let that change how we treat every person we meet this week. Amen.
reflection: Where have I treated the image of God in me as an achievement to defend rather than a gift I was given?
Who have I quietly ranked as less than fully human, and what standard have I been using to do it?
If a human being is set in the world to show what God is like, what has my life been showing about him?
sessions.teaching:
The first thing to understand about this sentence is how dangerous it was to say out loud. "Then God said, 'Let us make man in our image, after our likeness'" (Genesis 1:26). We hear a warm compliment, a pat on the human head, and hearing it that way we miss almost everything. In the world it was first spoken into, it was closer to sedition than to flattery.

The great civilizations around ancient Israel had their own ways of speaking about a divine image, and they kept it in the palace. In Egypt the Pharaoh could be called the image of the god, the god's living likeness on earth. In Mesopotamia the king could be called the god's image, set on earth as the god's representative, and ordinary people weren't. The image was a title of empire. It said that one man at the top carried the divine on his face, and the farmers and slaves and women and conquered peoples existed to serve him.

That's the world Genesis 1 walks into, and it takes the most exclusive idea in the ancient Near East and gives it away. "So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them" (Genesis 1:27). Not the king. The human being as such: the slave who owns nothing, the woman the culture treated as property, the infant who has done nothing, the enemy across the river. J. Richard Middleton, in his study of Genesis 1, calls this "the liberating image," and the phrase is exact. Genesis strips the divine dignity from the one and gives it to all.

The word itself carries the point. The Hebrew is tselem, and elsewhere it's used for a statue, the kind of image a people would set up to represent their god, where you went to see what the god was like. Genesis says the human being is God's image, set not in a stone temple but in the whole of his creation, placed here to represent him and to show the watching world what the true King is like. So from the first page the image isn't mainly a fact about what's inside you. It's a calling. It's the dignity of being the one creature commissioned to stand for God in the world he made. That's why image and dominion arrive together: "Let us make man in our image... And let them have dominion" (Genesis 1:26).

A thoughtful skeptic will push back, and he deserves a fair hearing. The modern reduction says all this is a flattering story a clever animal tells itself. Human beings are one species among many, produced by the same process, formed of the same stuff, running on the same instincts. I came to faith from atheism, so I know that answer from the inside. There's a lot of truth in it, and Scripture says it first. "The LORD God formed the man of dust from the ground" (Genesis 2:7). We're creatures, mortal and made of dirt, and the Bible never pretends otherwise.

But watch where the reduction breaks, because it breaks on the person who holds it. Nobody who says a human is only a clever animal lives that way for one waking hour. He's outraged by cruelty, grieved at a graveside, certain that a child is worth more than a stone and that some things must never be done to a person however useful they'd be. None of that follows from his premise. You can't get boundless human worth out of atoms and appetite. The image is the missing explanation, the one account that makes sense of the dignity all of us already assume and none of us can build from below. The psalmist felt both halves: "What is man that you are mindful of him... Yet you have made him a little lower than the heavenly beings and crowned him with glory and honor" (Psalm 8:4-5).

Then the doctrine turns on us. It doesn't only rescue the beggar from our contempt; it exposes the contempt. Most of us assign worth on a sliding scale, generous toward the useful and impressive and the people who can do something for us, and dismissive toward the inconvenient and ordinary and the ones who cost us something. We treat our own dignity as something we earned and other people's as a grade we're entitled to give. The image won't allow either. It was given, not earned, to every human before any of us had done a thing, so we can't inflate our own and we can't mark down anyone else's. The kings kept the image for themselves. God gave it away. And before that gift comforts you, it takes out of your hand the ruler you've been using to measure other people.

scriptureStudy.note: "Let us make man in our image, after our likeness. And let them have dominion." Image and dominion arrive together, so representing God and ruling on his behalf are one calling. The human is made to stand for the King, not to be one.

"In the image of God he created him; male and female he created them." The verse says it twice for emphasis and puts male and female in the same image in the same breath, honoring exactly the half of humanity the ancient world discounted.

"Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth and subdue it." The blessing spreads the image across the whole race and down every generation. Dominion is given to all of them together, never to one ruler over the rest.

"The LORD God formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life." The creature who bears the image is made of dirt. Scripture holds dust and glory together without embarrassment, so the image never denies that we're creatures.

"The LORD God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to work it and keep it." The word for keep is used for guarding. Dominion in the image is stewardship on the King's behalf, answerable to him.

"What is man that you are mindful of him, and the son of man that you care for him? Yet you have made him a little lower than the heavenly beings and crowned him with glory and honor." The psalm marvels at the paradox: a creature of dust crowned with royal dignity by God's choice.

"You have given him dominion over the works of your hands; you have put all things under his feet." The royal calling of Genesis is sung back to God. It's a kingship given and held in trust under the true King.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants more, look further into the background, because the more you learn about the world Genesis was written into, the more startling the text becomes. In Egyptian and Mesopotamian royal ideology, the language of a divine image was used largely of the king, and it did political work, backing his rule as the earthly presence of the god. J. Richard Middleton, in The Liberating Image, argues in detail that Genesis 1 deliberately answers that ideology by taking the royal image and giving it to all humanity. A group that sits with his case will find the creation account far less tame than the usual reading. Notice too that the making of humans is told differently from everything else in Genesis 1: God deliberates, "Let us make man," marking the human as the high point of the ordered creation.

Weigh, carefully and without overreaching, how much of the modern conviction that all humans are equal in worth flows historically from this text, since the ancient world it entered didn't hold that idea and it had to come from somewhere. And notice that even here the image is presented less as something humans possess than as a status God assigns and a task God gives. That quietly guards against the trap the doctrine most often falls into, grounding human worth in a capacity some people have more of than others. That's the work of the next session.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a man in your group is successful and capable and runs his whole life on merit. When the session lands on the image as a given, unearned dignity, he doesn't argue, but you can see it isn't reaching him. He has always assumed, without saying it, that a person is worth what they contribute. He's generous and works hard, and he doesn't see that his generosity can be a kind of condescension, help handed down by a man privately sure he's worth more.

Honor him before you press him. His diligence is real and good, and the world needs people who carry weight. But notice the ruler he's using. The merit standard that inflates his own worth is the same one that quietly discounts everyone who produces less: the disabled, the elderly, the struggling, the poor. The danger isn't that he values excellence. It's that he has grounded human dignity in a capacity, and any dignity grounded in a capacity can be lost, and will be denied to whoever falls below his line.

Don't let him reduce the doctrine to a nice sentiment he can affirm for free. Honor his work fully, and still ask him gently whether he could receive his own worth as a gift he didn't earn, because until he can, he'll keep grading everyone he meets.

sessions.title: What the Image Is, and Why the Argument Matters
sessions.aim: To learn the three classic answers to what the image is, the substantive, the functional and the relational, to see the strength and the danger in each, and to see that this isn't a seminary parlor game but the argument that decides who gets counted as fully human.
sessions.summary:
For most of its history the church has agreed that human beings bear the image of God and disagreed about what the image is. The disagreement matters, because your answer decides who you'll treat as fully human.

There are three classic answers. The substantive view says the image is a quality inside us, usually reason or the rational soul; it runs from Augustine and Aquinas through most of Christian history. The functional view says the image is a role, the calling to represent God and rule the creation as his stewards, and it fits the ancient background best. The relational view, associated above all with Karl Barth and Dietrich Bonhoeffer, finds the image in the relationships we're made for, with God and with one another.

The substantive view honors something real: humans reason and choose as animals don't. But it carries a danger. If the image is a capacity, then whoever has less of the capacity seems to have less of the image, and history is full of what follows when someone decides another group doesn't measure up. A calling can be given to a person who can't yet carry it out, and a relationship can hold a person who can't respond. The truest answer holds all three, in an order: what God gives and does comes before what we possess and perform. A gift can't be graded, and no one falls below the line.

keyScripture.why: "When God created man, he made him in the likeness of God" (Genesis 5:1), and then Adam "fathered a son in his own likeness, after his image" (Genesis 5:3). The image passes from parent to child, given and inherited rather than achieved, which cuts against any view that ties it to a capacity a person might lack.

discussion.q: Before tonight, if someone had asked what the image of God is, what would you have said? Which view, a quality inside us, a role we're given, or a relationship we stand in, were you assuming without knowing it?
discussion.behind: Get the working answer out before naming the options. Most people assume the substantive view: the image means reason, soul or free will. Don't correct it yet. The point is that everyone already holds a view, and it has been shaping who they count as fully bearing God's image.

discussion.q: If the image is a capacity like reason, what happens to the person who has less of that capacity? Where have you seen that logic play out?
discussion.behind: Go carefully. This is tender ground where real families and real grief live. Help the room see the trap: grounding worth in a capacity means worth can be lost or denied. It's the logic behind treating the disabled, the person with dementia, the unborn or the enemy as less than human. Hold it gently, but don't soften the danger.

discussion.q: How do the functional and relational views protect the worth of someone who can't reason, in a way the substantive view struggles to?
discussion.behind: A calling can belong to someone who can't yet, or can no longer, carry it out. A relationship can hold someone who can't respond, the way a parent's love holds a newborn or a spouse keeps faith with someone lost to dementia. Help the room feel the difference between dignity that can be revoked and dignity that can't.

discussion.q: The truest answer holds all three views, with what God gives and does coming before what we possess and perform. Why does that order matter so much, and what goes wrong when we put our performance first?
discussion.behind: This is the center of the session. If the image is first a gift and a call from God, it can't be graded by our capacities, and every human holds it fully. Put the capacity first and we're back to ranking people. The order mirrors the whole gospel: grace before response, gift before work.

discussion.q: Whose full humanity do you find easiest to doubt: the person with severe disability, someone deep in dementia, a criminal, the unborn, an enemy? What view of the image have you been running to justify the doubt?
discussion.behind: Go first and name your own line. Everyone draws one somewhere and has a theory that lets them. Invite candor without shaming anyone, and let the room see that worth-by-capacity is usually the tool.

objections.objection: This is the kind of hairsplitting that makes people tune out. Does it matter whether the image is a quality or a role or a relationship, as long as we agree people have dignity?
objections.response: The impatience is aimed at a real vice: theology that argues over definitions while people starve, and the church has wasted itself on distinctions that changed nothing. This isn't one of them. The moment a society has to decide whether the person in a long coma, or the unborn child, or the prisoner, or the enemy is fully human and fully protected, it reaches for a theory of what makes a human count, whether it knows it or not. If the answer is a capacity, reason or self-awareness or usefulness, the line can always be moved, and history shows it always is, and the people on the wrong side are always the weak. The argument about what the image is turns out to be the argument about who lives with dignity and who can be discarded.

objections.objection: If the image is only a role or a relationship and not something actually in us, it sounds like empty words. Either humans really are different from animals in their nature, or the image is a label with nothing behind it.
objections.response: That instinct protects something true. There's a real difference between humans and animals, and the substantive view is right to insist on it. But the objection offers a false choice, as if a gift and a relationship were nothing. A newborn is fully a son or a daughter before she can do anything a child does, and that relationship isn't empty; it's the most real thing about her, and it holds when every capacity fails. The functional and relational views don't empty the image. They anchor it somewhere sturdier than a faculty that can be damaged or lost. And the deepest reason to prefer that anchor is love, because a dignity grounded only in capacity abandons exactly the people this doctrine was written to protect: the infant, the disabled and the dying.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Where have you been grounding your own worth, and the worth of people you love, in a capacity that can be lost, and what would it mean to ground it in what God gives and won't take back?
sessions.practice: This week, find the place where your own working theory of the image is doing quiet damage: a relative you've written off, a group you've decided counts for less, or yourself on the days you aren't producing. Name the standard you've been using, worth by capacity or worth by usefulness. Then deliberately treat one such person, or yourself, as fully bearing God's image regardless of what they can do. Write down what that showed you.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, you made us in your image, and we've spent centuries arguing about what that means, and somewhere in the arguing we found ways to decide that some people bear it more than others. Forgive us. Forgive the theories we've built to justify looking down on the weak, the slow, the unborn and the enemy. Teach us that the image is your gift before it's our possession and your call before it's our performance, so it can't be graded and no one falls below the line. Anchor our worth, and the worth of everyone we're tempted to discount, in what you give and won't take back. And where we've drawn a line through the middle of the human race, give us grace to erase it. Amen.
reflection: Which view of the image have I been living by without knowing it, and who does it let me discount?
Have I grounded human worth, mine and others', in a capacity that can be lost, or in what God gives and won't revoke?
Where is the line I've drawn between the fully human and the less-than, and what would it cost me to let this doctrine erase it?
sessions.teaching:
For most of its history the church has agreed on one thing and argued about another. It has agreed that human beings bear the image of God. It has argued about what the image actually is. It would be easy to file that under harmless disputes among theologians, except that it isn't harmless. The answer you give decides who you're willing to treat as fully human. So we need to walk slowly and fairly through the three classic answers, because each has held the loyalty of serious, faithful minds, and each sees something the others can miss.

The first is the substantive view, the historic majority. It says the image is a quality located inside the human being, and most often that quality is reason, the rational soul, the capacity to think and choose and know God. Augustine found the image in the mind, in memory, understanding and will. Thomas Aquinas located it in the intellect, the rational nature that sets humans apart from animals. There's real truth in this. Human beings do reason and create and deliberate as nothing else in the visible world does, and any account that denies it isn't being truthful about what a person plainly is.

But the substantive view carries a danger, and I want to name it plainly. If the image is a capacity like reason, then it comes in degrees, because capacities come in degrees. Some people have more and some have less. The infant who can't yet think, the man with dementia who no longer knows his own name, the child with a profound disability who will never form a sentence: on this logic each has less of the image, and the logic whispers, less of the worth. That isn't a hypothetical horror. It's the machinery of dehumanization again and again in history. Decide the image is a capacity and you've handed the powerful a ruler to measure the weak, and they always find them wanting.

That's why the other two views matter. The functional view, which fits the ancient background we saw last session, says the image is mainly a calling: to represent God and rule his creation as his stewards. A calling can be given to someone who can't presently carry it out. A king's infant son is fully the heir before he can lift the scepter.

The relational view is associated above all with Karl Barth and Dietrich Bonhoeffer. It locates the image not in what we possess but in the relationships we're made for, with God and with one another. Barth read "male and female" in Genesis 1:27 as the clue: the human isn't made to be alone but to be in relationship, answering to the relationship God himself is. Bonhoeffer lectured on Genesis in Berlin in 1932 and 1933, as the movement that would soon rank human lives by their supposed value was taking power. He refused to treat the image as a possession at all and described it as a relation God establishes, our being free for God and for one another. A relationship can hold a person who can't respond. A newborn is fully loved before she loves back. A husband keeps covenant with a wife who no longer knows him. If the image is first the relationship God establishes toward us, it holds when every human capacity has failed, because it never depended on the capacity.

I don't want to dismiss the majority of the church as simply wrong. Humans really do reason, that matters, and a purely functional or relational account can drift into vagueness if it denies anything distinctive in human nature. So the truest answer doesn't pick one view and throw out the others. It holds all three, but in an order. What God gives and does comes first; what we possess and perform comes after. The image is first a status God confers, a call God issues and a relationship God establishes, and only then the capacities by which we live it out. Paul speaks of the new self "being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator" (Colossians 3:10), honoring what the substantive view saw while making clear it's something grace renews, not something we generate.

Keep that order and the doctrine is safe, because a gift can't be graded, a call doesn't depend on the strength to answer it, and a relationship holds the one who can't respond. Reverse it and you're back to ranking human beings by their faculties. Most of us run the reversed order in our own hearts more than we'd like to admit, quick to see the full humanity of people who can think alongside us and slow to see it in those who can't. Genesis has already answered. "When God created man, he made him in the likeness of God" (Genesis 5:1), and Adam "fathered a son in his own likeness, after his image" (Genesis 5:3). The image went to the child before the child had done a thing, passed down like a family face, given and never earned.

scriptureStudy.note: "When God created man, he made him in the likeness of God." Written after the fall, the verse still speaks of humanity in God's likeness, stated as a plain given about the human race, not a prize for the capable.
"He fathered a son in his own likeness, after his image, and named him Seth." The image passes from parent to child like a family face, received before the child can do anything.
"For God made man in his own image." Spoken to Noah after the flood, over a sinful humanity, it grounds the protection of every human life in the image, not in merit or ability.

"For you formed my inward parts; you knitted me together in my mother's womb. I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made." The psalmist's worth rests on God's making and knowing him, before any capacity he could exercise.

"With it we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God." James assumes that ordinary, fallen people still bear the likeness. That's why cursing them is an offense.

"The new self, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator." Paul ties the image to knowing God, honoring what the substantive view saw, while making it something grace renews rather than something we produce.

"God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong; God chose what is low and despised in the world, even things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are." God's habit of lifting the discounted undoes every scheme that ranks human worth by capacity.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants more, trace the history of the three views, because knowing where each came from helps a group hold them without caricature. The substantive reading dominated from the early church through the Middle Ages and into the Reformation. Augustine found a trinitarian pattern in the soul, memory, understanding and will, and Aquinas grounded the image in the rational intellect. They were honoring something real, the way human reason is turned toward God, not merely flattering the clever. The functional view is the one much modern Old Testament scholarship, Middleton included, judges closest to Genesis 1 in its own world, and a group can ask how far the older reading was shaped by Greek philosophical categories brought to the text.

The relational view is a twentieth-century recovery, and the reading can't be separated from its moment. Barth developed it in his Church Dogmatics in the 1940s, and Bonhoeffer gave the lectures published as Creation and Fall in Berlin in 1932 and 1933, as a regime that would rank human lives by their supposed worth came to power. Those recoveries weren't academic fashion. In part they were resistance: relocating human dignity somewhere a state couldn't reach it, out of the capacities a regime could measure and into the gift and call of God. Then test the claim this study makes: the tradition went wrong most often not by choosing the wrong view but by putting human capacity first in the order.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a woman in your group has a brother in his forties with a profound intellectual disability. He can't speak or care for himself and will never do what the world calls productive work. She has sat through years of Christian talk about the image of God as reason and rationality, and every time something in her has gone cold, because she heard it, correctly, as a doctrine that left her brother out. When this session names the danger in the substantive view, she doesn't feel attacked. For the first time, she feels defended.

Your work here is mostly to let the doctrine do its healing. Don't rush past her to be balanced. Honor what she has seen more clearly than many theologians: a worth grounded in capacity is a worth her brother can never have, and that isn't a small flaw in the view but a wound it has given families like hers.

Then let her hear the functional and relational answer as the good news it is. Her brother bears the image of God fully. He was given a status he didn't earn and is held in a relationship with God he didn't start and can't lose. He doesn't have less of the image because he can do less. Let her carry that home, and let the room learn from her that this argument was never abstract to the people it protects.
