sessions.title: Defaced but Not Destroyed
sessions.aim: To face the fall squarely, to see what sin did to the image and what it couldn't do, and to hold together two truths the church keeps pulling apart: the image is real and badly marred, and it was never erased, so human dignity survives even our worst.
sessions.summary:
The doctrine of the image has two enemies sitting on opposite sides of the room. One is so impressed with human dignity that it can't take sin seriously. The other is so impressed with human sin that it forgets the dignity. The fall is where both go wrong.

What did sin do to the image? Scripture's answer has two sides. The image was defaced. Genesis 3 isn't a small stumble. The creature made to represent God reached to be God, and the damage touched everything: reason, will, and every relationship the image was made to hold. Some faithful readers conclude the image is as good as gone. That reading is defending the seriousness of sin, and the church has often been far too cheerful about human nature.

But it breaks on Scripture itself. After the fall, after the flood, God still calls the human being his image: "for God made man in his own image" (Genesis 9:6). James says we "curse people who are made in the likeness of God" (James 3:9), meaning ordinary sinful people now. The image is defaced, and it isn't destroyed. What survives is a ruined greatness. It explains why human evil is so terrible, and why no one, however far gone, is ever beyond worth or beyond hope.

keyScripture.why: "Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed, for God made man in his own image" (Genesis 9:6). Spoken to a world just judged for its violence, it grounds the protection of every remaining sinful life in an image the fall marred but never erased.

discussion.q: One error takes human dignity so seriously it forgets sin; the other takes sin so seriously it forgets dignity. Which is more natural to you, and how does it come out in you?
discussion.behind: Help each person find their own tilt. Some are natural optimists about people and flinch at the word sin. Others are so convinced of human corruption they can barely see any glory left. Both are half-truths, and the fall is where they have to correct each other.

discussion.q: Genesis 9 grounds the command against murder in the image of God, and it says this to survivors of a flood sent because of human violence. Why does God protect the sinner by pointing to the image, and what does that tell you about how far the image survives?
discussion.behind: Press on where the verse sits. God has just judged the earth for its wickedness, and almost the first thing he does is protect human life by appealing to the image in people who have proved capable of terrible evil. The image isn't a reward for the righteous; it's a status that stays with the sinner.

discussion.q: Some readers say sin has corrupted the image almost to nothing. What is that reading rightly protecting, and what does Scripture say that it can't account for?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves. The dark reading defends the seriousness of sin against a sentimental culture that won't name evil, and it's right that nothing in us was left untouched. But it can't account for Genesis 9 and James 3, which speak of the image in fallen people now. Grant the seriousness; refuse the conclusion that the image is gone.

discussion.q: If human beings are something like defaced royalty, a ruined greatness, how does that change the way you understand both human evil and human worth?
discussion.behind: Human evil is so terrible because image-bearers commit it; it's greatness gone wrong, not an animal following instinct. Human worth survives because the image, though marred, remains. Help the room see that the ruin and the dignity don't compete; they explain each other.

discussion.q: Is there a person, or a version of yourself, you've quietly written off as beyond worth or beyond change? What has believing that let you do, or stop doing?
discussion.behind: Go gently, because this can touch real despair, and go first with your own too-far-gone verdict. Writing someone off, including ourselves, is always a denial that the image survives. Be careful with anyone carrying shame or grieving someone lost to addiction or hardness. Let the truth that the image isn't destroyed land as hope, and keep a path to real help visible: a pastor, a counselor, and the guide's help information.

objections.objection: How can you say people still bear the image of God after everything human beings do to each other? Genocide, cruelty, abuse. If that's the image of God, the image is either a lie or an insult to God.
objections.response: Don't argue with the horror. The objection isn't cynical; it's facing evil more squarely than sentimental people do. Human cruelty is real, and worse than any of us can say, and any doctrine that makes light of it is false. But notice what the objection assumes: that this cruelty is a horror at all. We aren't outraged when a spider eats its mate, because we expect nothing else of a spider. We're undone by human cruelty because we know, underneath our theories, that a human being was made for more. This is greatness in ruins, not an animal being an animal. The image is what makes human evil so terrible. A defaced masterpiece grieves us in a way a blank wall never could. The evil doesn't disprove the image. It desecrates it, and the grief you feel is the image in you recognizing the ruin of the image in them.

objections.objection: This sounds like letting people off the hook. If everyone keeps this precious image no matter what they do, where's the accountability? It seems to excuse the worst behavior by insisting on a hidden dignity underneath.
objections.response: A cheap dignity that excused evil would be a moral disaster, and Scripture never offers one. The image doesn't lessen guilt; it deepens it. To sin as an image-bearer is worse than to sin as an animal, because it betrays what you were made to be, and the murder condemned in Genesis 9 is condemned precisely because the victim bore the image. So the doctrine is the ground of taking evil seriously. What the surviving image refuses isn't accountability but despair: the verdict that a person is finished, beyond worth and beyond hope, fit only to be discarded. You can hold someone fully accountable for what they did, and protect others from them, and still refuse to say they're no longer human. Justice names the wrong. The image insists the wrongdoer is still someone God made and still not beyond the reach of his mercy.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Where has your sense of your own failure convinced you that the image in you is destroyed rather than defaced, and what would change if you believed God still sees his likeness in you?
sessions.practice: This week, hold together the two truths this session won't separate. Toward one person you've been too soft on, yourself included, name the sin plainly instead of excusing it, because the image makes evil serious. Toward one person you've written off as beyond change or beyond worth, refuse that verdict, and treat them as a defaced image rather than a finished ruin. Write down which was harder for you, because the harder one shows which of the two errors is yours.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we come as your defaced image, and we don't know which is harder to believe: that we're so ruined, or that we're still yours. We've taken the greatness you gave us and turned it against you and against each other, and the wreckage is real; we won't pretend it's small. But you haven't let go of your likeness in us. You protected even the sinner by pointing to the image he still bore, and you've never looked at a human being and called them past worth or past hope. Give us sight with both eyes open, to name evil for the desecration it is and to refuse to write off anyone you haven't written off. Where we've despaired of ourselves or of someone we love, remind us that a defaced image isn't a destroyed one, and that you restore what we ruined. Amen.
reflection: Do I take sin seriously enough to grieve it, or do I explain evil away because I'm so impressed with human dignity?
Do I take the image seriously enough to refuse to write anyone off, or am I so impressed with human sin that I forget the dignity that survives?
Where have I believed the image in me is destroyed rather than defaced, and what has that despair cost me and the people around me?
sessions.teaching:
The doctrine of the image has two enemies, and they sit on opposite sides of the same room, each sure the other is the only danger. On one side is the person so impressed with human dignity that he can't take sin seriously. He hears the word depravity as an insult and believes, at bottom, that people are basically good and only need the right conditions. On the other side is the person so impressed with human sin that he has forgotten the dignity. He has read the news and read his own heart and concluded that talk of a divine image is a pious fiction laid over something rotten. The fall is exactly where both go wrong, because Scripture's account of what sin did to the image is careful and two-sided and comforts neither of them.

So what did sin actually do to the image of God in us? The first part of the answer is that the image was defaced, and that isn't too strong a word. Genesis 3 isn't a small misstep in an otherwise upward climb. The serpent's promise was "you will be like God" (Genesis 3:5). The creature made to represent God reached to replace him, and nothing was left untouched. Reason, meant to know God, now rationalizes and deceives. The will, meant to love God, curves in on itself. Every relationship the image was made to hold broke the same afternoon. "The man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God" (Genesis 3:8). They blamed each other, and they were sent out of the garden. And the next chapter tells us that "Cain rose up against his brother Abel and killed him" (Genesis 4:8). Anyone who says the fall was minor hasn't read the account, or himself.

Some faithful Christians have taken the darkest reading of all: the corruption runs so deep that the image is effectively gone, a ruin not worth the name. I want to grant what that reading protects. It protects the seriousness of sin against a culture, and a church, that will do almost anything to avoid the word. We're sentimental about human nature in a way that would have baffled earlier Christian centuries, and the dark reading is cold water we need.

But it breaks, and not on my preference. It breaks on the plain words of Scripture. After the fall, after the whole race has shown what it is, after a flood sent because "the earth was filled with violence" (Genesis 6:11), God speaks to the survivors and grounds the sanctity of human life in the image, in these sinners: "Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed, for God made man in his own image" (Genesis 9:6). If the image were destroyed, that sentence would make no sense. Centuries later James, writing to Christians about their tongues, says "we curse people who are made in the likeness of God" (James 3:9). He means ordinary sinful people, right now. Paul can say that "all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God" (Romans 3:23), the glory we were made to bear. So hold both truths, because the pastoral weight of the doctrine hangs on them together. The image is defaced. The image isn't destroyed.

The dignity that survives isn't a happy scrap of leftover goodness we can feel good about. It's stranger than that and more useful: a wound and a signature at once, defaced royalty. Seen that way, two things come clear. First, you understand why human evil is so specifically terrible, why cruelty undoes us in a way a predator killing its prey doesn't. Human evil is greatness gone wrong, a masterpiece slashed, and grief is the right response to a desecration.

Second, you understand why no human being is beyond worth or beyond hope. If the image were destroyed, some people really could be written off, and most of us keep a private list of exactly those people. But a defaced image is still an image. The signature is still under the ruin. The worst person you know, and the worst version of yourself you've buried in shame, isn't finished.

Here the doctrine raises a question it can't answer by itself. A defaced image can survive, but it can't repair itself. For that we need not a better version of ourselves but the true image, the one who came to make the ruined ones new.

scriptureStudy.note: "You will be like God, knowing good and evil." The fall is the image-bearer reaching to be God rather than to represent him, the calling turned upside down at the root.

"The man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God among the trees of the garden." The first fruit of the fall is a broken relationship, so sin strikes the image right where the relational view says it lives.
"Cain rose up against his brother Abel and killed him." Within a generation one image-bearer spills another's blood. The ruin is real and reaches the first family God made.
"For God made man in his own image." Spoken after the flood over sinful survivors, it shows the fall didn't destroy the image, since the protection of human life still rests on it.

"Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me." David names how deep the corruption goes without ever concluding he isn't God's. He holds the seriousness of sin and his standing before God together.
"For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God." The glory we fall short of is the glory we were made to bear, so the verse assumes both the original dignity and its present ruin.

"With it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God... My brothers, these things ought not to be so." James assumes fallen people still bear the likeness, and he makes that the reason our contempt for them is sin. The image protects the sinner from us.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants more, look at the vocabulary the church developed to hold this two-sided truth. Reformed theologians after Calvin spoke of the image in a broad sense and a narrow sense. The broad image is the human constitution that survives the fall: reason, conscience, relationship, the calling to rule. The narrow image is the original righteousness, knowledge and holiness that were lost and are restored only in Christ. With that distinction a group can see how Scripture says both that the image remains (Genesis 9, James 3) and that it must be renewed (Colossians 3, Ephesians 4) without contradicting itself. Calvin himself wrote in the Institutes that the image wasn't wholly destroyed but was so corrupted that what remains is a frightful deformity, a phrase that holds the balance this session is after.

Set beside that the older debate over "image" and "likeness." Some early theologians read them as two different things, the image kept and the likeness lost. Most modern interpreters think that reads too much into a Hebrew pairing of near-synonyms, and a group can ask why the church sometimes built large structures on small grammatical foundations. Then test the claim that both errors have real consequences. A theology that forgets the fall produces a church that can't name evil and offers the guilty cheap comfort, the therapeutic religion that has become the working faith of much of our culture. A theology that forgets the surviving image produces a church that writes people off: the addict, the prisoner, the enemy.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a man in your group carries a heavy, specific shame. Years ago he did something he considers unforgivable, a betrayal that cost him his marriage and his children's trust. He has been a believer since, but he has quietly concluded that whatever he was made to be, he destroyed it. When the session insists the image is marred and never erased, you can see him resist, because his despair has become a strange comfort, a way of not having to hope.

Go gently and don't hurry him past his grief. Don't minimize what he did; the doctrine doesn't, and a cheap word would insult both his conscience and the people he hurt. But press kindly on the lie inside his despair: that he has the power to destroy what God made and protects. That's an odd form of pride, as if his sin were stronger than God's likeness. It isn't. The image in him is ruined, not gone, and a ruined image is exactly what the true image came to restore.

Keep a path to real help in front of him: a pastor or a counselor who can walk with him, and the help information printed with this guide if the shame has turned into something darker. Honor the weight he carries, and still refuse, on God's behalf, to agree that he's finished, because God hasn't agreed to it.

memoryVerse.text: This is the book of the generations of Adam. When God created man, he made him in the likeness of God.

sessions.title: The True Image, and the One We Are Becoming
sessions.aim: To see that the doctrine of the image was always pointing to Christ, who doesn't only bear the image but is the image, and to grasp that salvation is the defaced image being remade into his likeness, so that Christian formation is becoming truly human at last.
sessions.summary:
The doctrine of the image can't be finished in Genesis, because it was never meant to end there. Adam was made in the image. Christ is the image. That difference is the gospel. Paul doesn't say Jesus bears the image well. He says Christ "is the image of the invisible God" (Colossians 1:15), the one in whom the unseen God is finally made visible.

That runs in two directions. Backward, it tells us that humanity was patterned after the Son from the beginning. Forward, it tells us where salvation is going: believers are "predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son" (Romans 8:29), changed "into the same image from one degree of glory to another" (2 Corinthians 3:18).

Some hear that as self-improvement, becoming a better version of yourself, and the church has often preached it that way. But the difference is total. This isn't the self polishing the self. It's the defaced image being restored by the true image, from outside, by grace, and the means Paul names is beholding, not striving. Being saved isn't becoming something other than human. It's becoming human at last. The image was defaced in a garden; it's restored in a person.

keyScripture.why: "He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation" (Colossians 1:15). Christ isn't one more image-bearer but the image itself, the one in whom the unseen God is made visible, and the pattern into which the defaced human image is being remade.

discussion.q: Paul says Christ is the image of the invisible God, not merely someone who bears it well. What changes when you hear that Jesus is the original, and Adam and you are the likeness?
discussion.behind: We tend to think of Jesus as the best example of an image-bearer, the human who got it right. Paul says something stronger. Help the room feel that this makes Christ not our best member but our source and pattern, which reframes both who Jesus is and who we are.

discussion.q: What changes in your sense of the Christian life if being conformed to Christ is the same thing as becoming truly human?
discussion.behind: Many people quietly assume holiness means becoming less themselves: more restrained, more religious. Scripture says it means becoming what humanity was always meant to be. Help the room hear formation as restoration, not subtraction, so the most Christlike person is also the most fully human.

discussion.q: Paul says we're changed into his image "from one degree of glory to another" by "beholding the glory of the Lord" (2 Corinthians 3:18). Why beholding, and not mainly striving? What does it mean that we become like what we look at?
discussion.behind: Press on the means, because it cuts against the works instinct. Paul grounds the change in fixing our gaze on Christ, because we become like what we worship and attend to. Ask the room what they actually look at all day, screens, ambitions, fears, and what that might be forming them into.

discussion.q: This can sound like self-improvement with Bible verses attached. Where is that reading tempting, and what makes restoration by Christ different from polishing the self?
discussion.behind: Let the group feel the pull of the self-help reading; the vocabulary really does overlap. But the source is outside us: Christ restoring his own defaced image by grace, not the self improving the self by effort. One ends in exhaustion or pride, the other in gratitude and rest.

discussion.q: Where do you see grace actually remaking you, and where are you still trying to do it yourself by striving rather than beholding?
discussion.behind: Go first and name where you're still white-knuckling it. Everyone has places where grace is visibly at work and places where they're grinding at their own improvement and calling it holiness. Don't shame the striving; point the room back toward looking at Christ rather than at themselves.

objections.objection: Being conformed to the image of Christ sounds like religious self-improvement with extra steps. Every self-help book tells you to become your best self. This is the same project in Bible language.
objections.response: From outside they can look identical. Both talk about change and growth, and the church has often preached holiness as a self-help seminar with prayer attached, so the suspicion is earned. But they're opposites at the root. Self-improvement is the self working on the self, the same broken thing straining to fix itself, and it ends either in the exhaustion of failure or the pride of apparent success. Both are prisons. Paul describes something running the other way. The self doesn't restore the image; the true image restores it, from outside, by grace, and the means is beholding: "we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image" (2 Corinthians 3:18). One is a mirror where you watch yourself and try harder. The other is a window through which you look at Christ and are slowly remade by what you see. The difference isn't the amount of effort. It's where the power comes from.

objections.objection: If we're all being conformed to Jesus, doesn't that erase individuality? It sounds like the goal is for every Christian to become an identical copy of the same person, which is the conformity that makes religion frightening.
objections.response: That fear is real, and some religion has earned it by producing people who are eerily the same, their edges sanded into one approved shape. That's a genuine distortion. But look at what likeness to Christ actually produces. When the image is restored, people don't become less themselves; they become more. Sin is the great flattener. It makes us predictable in our selfishness, all running the same tired scripts of pride and fear. A person set free from protecting and promoting himself is finally free to be the particular, unrepeatable person God made. The saints aren't identical. They're among the most vividly themselves of anyone who has lived. Christ isn't a cookie cutter pressed onto every face. He's the source in which each face becomes fully its own.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What are you actually looking at most hours of your day, and if you become like what you behold, what are you slowly being formed into?
sessions.practice: This week, change one thing you look at. Take a stretch of time you'd normally give to a screen or a worry, and spend it looking at Christ in one of the Gospels, reading slowly, watching how he treats people. Let your attention rest on him rather than on yourself. Don't turn it into a project you grade. Write down whether it's harder for you to stop striving and simply look, and what that says about where you've been trying to fix yourself by effort.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord Jesus, you are the image of the invisible God, the one Adam was made to resemble, and you wore our flesh without ruining it, and now you're remaking the ruin in us. Forgive us for turning your work of grace into a self-improvement project, standing at the mirror trying to fix ourselves when you called us to look at you and be changed. We become like what we look at, and we've been looking at everything but you. Turn our eyes. Restore your image in us, not by our striving but by your grace, from one degree of glory to another, until we're what you made us to be: truly human, fully alive, unmistakably ourselves and unmistakably yours. We can't repair what we ruined. You can, and you are. Amen.
reflection: Have I treated the Christian life as self-improvement, or as Christ restoring his likeness in me by grace?
What do I actually look at all day, and what is it forming me into?
Where am I straining at the mirror when Christ is calling me to look at him and be changed?
sessions.teaching:
Everything in this study has been building toward a name. Genesis 1 gives us the image made, Genesis 3 the image defaced, and if that were the whole story it would be a tragedy with no third act. But the New Testament takes up the word image and attaches it to a person. Adam was made in the image of God. Christ, Paul says, is the image of God. That small difference, "made in" against "is," is the gospel.

Listen to how strongly the New Testament says it, because we soften it out of habit. Paul doesn't say Jesus bears the image well or reflects it more clearly than the rest of us. He says, "He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation" (Colossians 1:15). He speaks of "the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God" (2 Corinthians 4:4). Hebrews says he is "the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature" (Hebrews 1:3). That isn't the language of a good copy. When Philip asked to see the Father, Jesus answered, "Whoever has seen me has seen the Father" (John 14:9). The God no one has seen is made visible in Jesus, not approximately but truly.

That runs in two directions. Run it backward first. If Christ is the image, then Adam was always the likeness, and humanity was patterned after the Son before the Son ever took our flesh. He isn't a rescue improvised after the fall. He's the pattern we were made from, which means the most human face that has ever existed is his, and every other human face is a likeness of it.

Now run it forward, because this is where the doctrine reaches into ordinary life. Paul says where salvation is going, and he says it in the language of the image. "Those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son" (Romans 8:29). Believers have put on "the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator" (Colossians 3:10). And then the most beautiful sentence of all: "And we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another" (2 Corinthians 3:18). The defaced image isn't left defaced. It's being restored into the likeness of the Son.

The obvious modern objection deserves a real answer. This sounds like self-improvement, one more program for becoming the best version of yourself, the same thing every book on the self-help shelf sells, with verses stapled on. The church has often preached it exactly that way, so the suspicion is fair. But the two are opposites at the root. Self-improvement is the self working on the self, the same defaced thing straining to repair itself, and it ends either in the exhaustion of failing or the pride of seeming to succeed. What Paul describes runs the other way. The self doesn't restore the image. The true image restores it, from outside, by grace.

And notice the means. It isn't striving; it's beholding. We're changed by looking at him. We become like what we look at, which is a thoroughly biblical idea; the psalm says of idols, "Those who make them become like them" (Psalm 115:8). That makes this the most practical part of the whole doctrine, because it means the question of your formation is largely the question of your attention. What are you looking at, hour after hour? You're being slowly shaped by it. The self-improver stands at a mirror, watching himself, grading, trying harder, and stays the same tired self. The Christian stands at a window, looking at Christ, and is quietly remade by what he sees.

Then the point I most want to leave with you. We think of being saved as becoming religious, or better, or something other than what we are. It's none of those. To be conformed to the image of Christ is to become human at last. Sin is what made us less than human, and its undoing isn't a religious layer added on top of a human life. It's the healing of the humanity itself. Paul says the restoration will be complete: "Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we shall also bear the image of the man of heaven" (1 Corinthians 15:49). The image was defaced in a garden by a creature grasping to be God. It's restored in a person, the true God who became the true man, who is even now remaking his likeness in everyone who looks to him.

scriptureStudy.note: "He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation." Christ isn't a bearer of the image but the image itself, the pattern after which humanity was made and into which it's being remade.

"The light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God." The gospel is the image shining out, and the god of this world works to blind people to it. Salvation means coming to see God's image in Christ.

"He is the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature." The word for imprint describes the mark a seal leaves, an exact impression. Christ isn't a rough likeness of God but the precise expression of who God is.
"Predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, in order that he might be the firstborn among many brothers." Likeness to the Son is the goal of salvation, not a side effect of it.
"Beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another." The change comes by looking, not straining, and it's gradual, glory to glory.
"The new self, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator." Salvation is the renewal of the image, present and ongoing, done by grace and never finished in a day.

"Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we shall also bear the image of the man of heaven." The restoration is final as well as present, completed at the resurrection, the ruined likeness not only repaired but glorified.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants more, trace the thread that ties the image to Christ across Scripture. Paul draws it most clearly in Romans 5 and 1 Corinthians 15, where Adam is the first man and Christ "the last Adam" (1 Corinthians 15:45), the head of a new humanity. The image defaced in the first is restored in the second. Followed through, the doctrine of the image stops being a static fact about human nature and becomes a story with a beginning, a rupture and a restoration, with Christ at the center as both origin and goal. Notice too that the New Testament never says Christ was made in the image, as Genesis says of Adam. It says he is the image.

Then take up the idea that we become like what we behold. It isn't a modern psychological insight bolted onto the text. It runs from the psalm about idol-makers becoming like their idols (Psalm 115:8), through Paul's beholding in 2 Corinthians 3, to John's promise that "we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is" (1 John 3:2). Sit with the sobering other side: the same law that conforms us to Christ as we look at him deforms us into the likeness of whatever else we worship. An economy built to capture and fracture our attention isn't spiritually neutral. It's forming people. Ask each person what they're actually beholding, since that's what they're becoming.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a woman in your group is one of the most disciplined believers you know, and she's exhausted. She reads her Bible on a strict schedule, tracks her habits and measures her growth, treating holiness like a fitness plan. She heard sermons on being conformed to Christ as marching orders, one more standard to meet. The striving has left her weary and quietly joyless, because however hard she works, the self she watches in the mirror never becomes what she's aiming at.

Honor her devotion before you redirect it. Her hunger for God is real, and her discipline isn't the problem. Don't shame it; a lazy alternative would help no one. But notice where her gaze is fixed. She's at the mirror, watching herself and grading her progress, and the whole weight of her formation rests on her own effort. That's self-improvement dressed as sanctification, and it will exhaust her because it was never meant to carry that weight.

Don't tell her to try less. Tell her to look somewhere else: to move from the mirror to the window, from watching herself improve to looking at Christ, and to trust that the change comes from him, by grace, from one degree of glory to another. She was never the one holding it together.

memoryVerse.text: And we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another.

sessions.title: The Image in the Street
sessions.aim: To bring the doctrine down into daily life, where it lives or dies, and to see that if every human being bears the image of God, then the poor, the unborn, the enemy, the stranger and the person who annoys you carry a worth we didn't assign and can't revoke, so that how we treat them is how we treat their Maker.
sessions.summary:
The doctrine of the image is either the most practical thing in the Bible or it's nothing, because a truth about human worth that never reaches the street was never really believed. The question isn't whether we affirm the image but whether we can see it in the faces we'd rather not. James puts the point sharply: with the same tongue "we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God" (James 3:9). We don't notice the contradiction, because the person we're cursing doesn't look like the image to us.

So this session walks through the people the image most inconveniently covers. The poor: "Whoever oppresses a poor man insults his Maker" (Proverbs 14:31). The unborn, whom God knits together in the womb, a subject the study handles with care for anyone in the room carrying a crisis. The enemy, whom Jesus commands us to love. The stranger, whom Israel was told to love as themselves. And the person who simply annoys us, maybe the hardest of all.

Some say this is politically convenient for one side. It isn't. The image cuts against every tribe with the same blade. If the image is real, there are no ordinary people and no faces safe to despise.

keyScripture.why: "With it we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God" (James 3:9). We honor God with our words and dishonor his image in the next breath, and rarely notice that it's the same tongue.

discussion.q: James says we bless God and curse people made in his likeness with the same tongue, and don't notice. Whose face doesn't look like the image of God to you, and what lets you curse them without feeling you've done anything wrong?
discussion.behind: Put the point where James puts it. We don't openly deny the image; we contradict it without noticing, because certain people don't register as image-bearers. Help the room name the specific kind of person they discount.

discussion.q: The poor, the unborn, the enemy, the stranger, the person who annoys you: which is hardest for you to see the image in, and why that one?
discussion.behind: Get specific, because the doctrine only bites at the level of the particular. Everyone has a hardest case, and it's usually the one their own circle has trained them to discount. Let each person name theirs without defending it right away.

discussion.q: Proverbs says whoever oppresses a poor man insults his Maker, and Jesus says what we did to "the least of these" we did to him (Matthew 25:40). What does it do to your treatment of the poor and overlooked to hear that you're treating their Maker that way?
discussion.behind: Scripture keeps saying that how you treat the image is how you treat the one it images. There's no such thing as a private unkindness to an image-bearer. Let that carry weight without collapsing into guilt that changes nothing.

discussion.q: The image cuts against every political tribe with the same blade, the side that discards the unborn and the side that discards the immigrant, the prisoner and the enemy. Where is it convenient for your side to forget the image, and can you name that as plainly as the other side's blind spot?
discussion.behind: This is the hardest question and the most necessary, and it has to cut both ways. Hold the room to naming the people their own side discards, not only their opponents'. Go first, and don't let the doctrine become a weapon for one team.

discussion.q: C. S. Lewis wrote, "You have never talked to a mere mortal." Who did you look past or look down on this week, and how would that encounter have gone if you'd seen them as the image of God?
discussion.behind: Bring it down to actual faces from an actual week: the clerk, the driver, the relative, the stranger. Let the room feel how many image-bearers they passed without seeing, and send them out carrying that rather than relieved of it.

objections.objection: Using the image of God to talk about the unborn or the immigrant is just baptizing a political agenda. It's religion picking a side in the culture war and pretending God signed its voting guide.
objections.response: That suspicion is often deserved. The image of God has been drafted into partisan projects on every side, quoted to win an argument rather than to see a person. But test the charge against what the doctrine does. A political agenda is selective, and the image isn't. One side forgets the image in the immigrant, the prisoner, the refugee and the enemy; the other forgets it in the unborn. The doctrine indicts both with the same blade, which no political tribe will do. If a teaching only ever convicts the other side, it has become a tribe in religious robes, and you're right to distrust it. But a doctrine that makes you defend the very people your own side discards isn't a political weapon. It refuses to let any tribe reduce a human being to their usefulness for its cause. The image doesn't take your side. It stands over every side and asks whether you can see the face your politics taught you to look past.

objections.objection: It's naive, even dangerous, to talk about seeing the image of God in your enemy. Some people are truly evil and want to do harm, and telling victims to see the divine image in their abuser is how the church has kept people trapped in danger.
objections.response: Grant this immediately and completely. The warning protects real and vulnerable people, and any teaching that uses the image to send a victim back into harm is a wicked distortion of it. Seeing the image in someone doesn't mean trusting them, staying within their reach, or failing to protect yourself and others from them. Where there's abuse, the faithful thing is safety, distance and real help, not a sentimental blindness that calls itself love. If that's where you are, the help information with this guide is for you. But the doctrine draws a distinction that keeps love from turning into either denial or hatred. Seeing the image in an enemy doesn't mean pretending they aren't dangerous. It means refusing to let even a real enemy become less than human in your eyes, a thing rather than a person, because once that happens you've begun to lose your own humanity to the hatred. You can name someone's evil plainly, protect yourself from it fully, work for justice against it, and still remember that the one who does it is a defaced image-bearer and not a mere monster. That refusal keeps the fight against evil from turning you into it.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Whose face have you let your politics, your fear or your grievance erase, so that they no longer register as the image of God, and what would it cost you to see them again?
sessions.practice: This week, take the one kind of person from this session you found hardest, the poor, the unborn, the enemy, the stranger, or the person who simply annoys you, and do one concrete thing that treats that person as the image of God rather than as a problem, a threat or part of the scenery. Not a grand gesture; one real act of seeing. If the hardest one is close to home, a relative or a coworker, start there. Write down what it showed you about yourself.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we bless you with our mouths and curse your image in the next breath, and we don't even notice. We've looked past the poor, looked down on the stranger, hardened ourselves against the enemy, and let the people who annoy us stop being people at all. We've let our tribes tell us which image-bearers count. Forgive us, and give us back our sight. Let us see your image in the clerk and the immigrant and the prisoner and the child not yet born and the enemy across every line we've drawn. Teach us that there are no ordinary people and no one we can treat with contempt without treating you that way. And where there's real danger, give us wisdom that protects without hating. Amen.
reflection: Whose full humanity have I let my tribe, my fear or my grievance erase, and can I name my own side's discarded people as plainly as my opponents'?
Do I believe that how I treat the image is how I treat the one it images, and would my week look different if I did?
How many image-bearers did I pass this week without seeing, and what would change if there really are no ordinary people?
sessions.teaching:
The doctrine of the image is either the most practical thing in the Bible or it's nothing, because a truth about human worth that lives comfortably in the head and never walks into the street was never actually believed. You can affirm the image of God in a small group and then go home and treat the drive-through worker like a vending machine, the relative you can't stand like bad weather, and the person across the political aisle like a category rather than a face. If you do, you didn't believe the doctrine. You only agreed with it, which is cheaper.

So this last session is the test, and the test isn't whether you can define the image but whether you can see it. James puts it sharply: "With it we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God. From the same mouth come blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so" (James 3:9-10). What should trouble us is that we don't feel the contradiction. We don't feel the whiplash of praising God and despising his image in the next breath, because the person we're cursing doesn't look like the image to us. Our eyes have been trained not to see it on certain faces.

So walk through those faces. Start with the poor, because Scripture is relentless here. "Whoever oppresses a poor man insults his Maker, but he who is generous to the needy honors him" (Proverbs 14:31). Jesus goes further than we're comfortable with: "as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me" (Matthew 25:40). There's no private contempt for a poor man. It travels straight up to the God whose image he is.

Then the unborn, and I want to handle this with care rather than as a slogan, because behind the abstraction are real women in real crisis, and the doctrine isn't served by cruelty. The psalmist says, "you knitted me together in my mother's womb... Your eyes saw my unformed substance" (Psalm 139:13, 16). God knew him there before he had reasoned a thought or been of use to anyone. That puts the worth of the unborn where we found the worth of the disabled and the dying in our second session: not on a capacity achieved but on a God who gives dignity before anyone can earn it. If worth waits on usefulness, the smallest lose it first.

Then the enemy. Jesus says, "Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven. For he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good" (Matthew 5:44-45). Seeing the image in an enemy isn't pretending they're safe. Where there's real danger, the faithful thing is protection and real help, not sentiment. But it is refusing to let even a real enemy become less than human in your eyes, because once that happens your hatred has begun to deface the image in you.

Then the stranger. Israel's law said, "You shall treat the stranger who sojourns with you as the native among you, and you shall love him as yourself, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt" (Leviticus 19:34). And last, maybe hardest, the person who simply annoys you: the coworker whose voice grates, the relative whose opinions exhaust you, the man talking too loudly three tables over. Contempt does its quiet work far below anything we'd call hatred, in the eye-roll and the sigh and the small dismissals by which we file a fellow image-bearer under nuisance.

The strongest objection says this is politically convenient: using the image to talk about the unborn or the immigrant is religion baptizing one side's agenda. I don't accept that, and here's why. The image cuts against every tribe with the same blade. It indicts the side that discards the immigrant, the prisoner and the enemy, and it indicts the side that discards the unborn, and it won't let either exempt itself. No political agenda does that, because agendas are selective. If a doctrine only ever convicts people you already disagree with, it has become a tribe in robes, and you should distrust it. The image forces you to defend the very people your own side has agreed to throw away. That includes me. The faces I find hard aren't random. They're the ones my own instincts and my own circle trained me to look past, and the doctrine keeps dragging my eyes back to them.

This doesn't end tidily, because this doctrine doesn't resolve. It convicts, and then it sends you out still carrying it. If the image is real, there are no ordinary people and no disposable ones. C. S. Lewis put it memorably in his 1941 sermon "The Weight of Glory": "There are no ordinary people. You have never talked to a mere mortal." He went on: "Next to the Blessed Sacrament itself, your neighbour is the holiest object presented to your senses." Every person you passed today, the one who annoyed you, the one you pitied, the one you feared and the one you didn't see at all, was the image of God, defaced and dignified, made and loved and known. One day we'll answer for how we saw them. So the question to carry out of these five weeks isn't whether you believe it. It's whose face you're going to go home and finally see.

scriptureStudy.note: "With it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God." James makes cursing a fellow human an offense against the image they bear, and exposes the unnoticed contradiction of blessing God and despising his likeness with the same tongue.
"Whoever oppresses a poor man insults his Maker, but he who is generous to the needy honors him." How we treat the poor reaches God, because the poor bear his image.

"Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed, for God made man in his own image." The sanctity of every human life, and the seriousness of taking it, rest on the image. It's a foundation, not a sentiment.

"You knitted me together in my mother's womb... Your eyes saw my unformed substance." God's knowing and forming of a person in the womb, before any capacity, grounds the worth of the smallest where every image-bearer's worth rests: in God's gift.

"Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven. For he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good." Jesus grounds love of enemies in the Father's own goodness toward those who oppose him.

"You shall treat the stranger who sojourns with you as the native among you, and you shall love him as yourself." The law extends the full dignity of the neighbor to the foreigner. Origin doesn't decide whose image is honored.

"As you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me." Jesus identifies himself with the hungry, the sick, the imprisoned and the stranger, so how we treat the least visible person is how we treat the King.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants more, look at how strange and fragile the claim of equal human dignity is. Historians and philosophers have traced how the conviction that all humans are equal in worth, now treated as obvious, grew in large part from the biblical doctrine of the image. The ancient world around the early church didn't hold that a slave and an emperor, a foreigner and a citizen, an infant and an adult were of equal worth. The idea had to be introduced against the grain. A group can weigh the argument, made by some secular thinkers as well, that a thoroughly secular account struggles to ground the very dignity it wants to keep.

Set that beside the twentieth century. Dietrich Bonhoeffer resisted a regime built on ranking human lives by their supposed worth, and Martin Luther King Jr. drew the case for civil rights from the image of God in every person. In each case the doctrine did political work by refusing to belong to a political tribe, indicting the powerful in the name of a dignity they hadn't given and couldn't take away. Then practice the discipline this study insists on: name the specific people your own political and cultural circle finds it convenient to discard, not only the ones your opponents discard. A doctrine of the image that changes no encounter on Monday was never believed on Sunday.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a woman in your group is warm, generous and committed to justice for the causes her community cares about. She speaks movingly about the dignity of the poor and the immigrant and the prisoner. When the session says the image cuts against every tribe and mentions the unborn in the same breath as the immigrant, you feel the room tighten. For her those belong to opposed moral worlds, and naming them together feels like betraying her side.

This needs the same even-handedness the doctrine asks for, and it starts by honoring her compassion. Her care for the discarded isn't a pose. It's real fruit of seeing the image, and you should say so warmly; a study that only convicted her side would be committing the very tribalism this session names. But the image doesn't respect the borders our tribes draw. The discipline she rightly applies to her opponents' blind spots is the one it now asks her to apply to her own.

Don't let her hear it as an ambush from the other team. Be just as ready to press the opposite blind spot in the man across the circle whose compassion runs strong for the unborn and thin for the prisoner and the enemy. Honor her love for the overlooked, and still ask her gently whether she can name her own side's discarded people as clearly as she names the other side's, because the image belongs to no party.

memoryVerse.text: With it we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God.

leaderPrimer:
The particular danger of a study on the image of God is that it's the easiest doctrine in the world to affirm and among the hardest to believe. A room can spend five weeks agreeing warmly that everyone bears the image while each person quietly exempts the people they find it convenient to discount. Left alone, the study turns into a group congratulating itself on a high view of human dignity in general without ever being made to see the face it looks past every Monday. So set the aim the first night and keep it: this isn't a study about human worth in general. It's about whether we can see the image of God in the poor, the unborn, the enemy, the stranger and the relative who exhausts us, and the only sight anyone in the room is responsible for is their own.

Guard against two failures. The first, and most likely, is tribal capture. The image of God has been drafted by every political side to defend the people it already wanted to defend and to indict only its opponents. Refuse that from the start, in both directions, and in your own heart first. A leader who aims the image at the other team and exempts his own will teach the room to do the same. The second failure is turning a doctrine of worth into a load of guilt that changes nothing. Keep driving the sessions down to real faces from a real week.

Take special care in two places. Session 3 touches real despair, people who have written themselves off as beyond worth or beyond change. Session 5 touches the unborn and the enemy, and there will almost certainly be people in the room carrying private grief: a crisis pregnancy in the family, a wound from an abuser, a loss. Keep a path to real help visible. Know a pastor and a counselor you can point to, keep the help information printed with this guide within reach, and point to Find Help on the site. Never let the doctrine be used to send anyone back into harm; seeing the image in a dangerous person never means staying within their reach.

Lead from inside the study, not above it. If you present yourself as the one who already sees every face rightly, the room will perform agreement back at you and nobody's eyes will open. Go in as someone still learning to see, still catching yourself looking past the image. Five weeks won't make anyone love perfectly. It can send a room home unable to look at another human being quite the same way again.

faq.q: Is this study going to get political, especially on things like abortion and immigration?
faq.a: It refuses to be captured by any political side, and that refusal is the discipline of the whole study. The doctrine of the image cuts against every tribe with the same blade. It indicts the side that discards the immigrant, the prisoner and the enemy, and the side that discards the unborn, and it won't let either exempt itself. Session 5 names this directly and asks the leader to press it in both directions, starting with their own side. The aim isn't a voting guide. It's a human dignity that stands over every party and belongs to none.

faq.q: What does the image of God actually mean? I've heard it my whole life and couldn't really explain it.
faq.a: You're in good company. The church has agreed for most of its history that humans bear the image and argued the whole time about what it is. Session 2 walks through the three classic answers. The substantive view says it's a quality inside us, usually reason or the soul. The functional view says it's a calling, to represent God and care for his creation. The relational view says it's found in the relationships we're made for, with God and with one another. Each sees something true. The study holds all three, but in an order: what God gives and does comes before what we possess and perform, so the image can't be graded by our abilities.

faq.q: Does the image of God survive after the fall, or did sin destroy it?
faq.a: Both truths have to be held. Sin defaced the image badly, touching reason, will and every relationship it was made to hold. But Scripture still calls fallen people God's image after the fall and after the flood (Genesis 9:6), and James says we curse "people who are made in the likeness of God" (James 3:9). The image is defaced, not destroyed. That explains why human evil is so terrible, and why no one is ever beyond worth or beyond hope.

faq.q: How is being conformed to Christ different from just self-improvement or becoming your best self?
faq.a: From outside they can look identical; at the root they're opposites. Self-improvement is the self working on the self, the same broken thing straining to fix itself, and it ends in exhaustion or pride. Paul describes the true image, Christ, restoring his defaced likeness in us by grace, and the means is beholding: we're "transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another" by "beholding the glory of the Lord" (2 Corinthians 3:18). The difference is where the power comes from.

faq.q: Why does the study say the image is a gift and not something we earn? Don't humans do things that show they bear it?
faq.a: We do show it, but the order matters, and getting it wrong is where the doctrine turns dangerous. If the image is first a capacity we have or a performance we give, it comes in degrees, and whoever has less seems to be worth less. If it's first something God gives and does, it can't be graded, and every human holds it fully. Scripture points that way: Adam passes the image to his son "in his own likeness, after his image" (Genesis 5:3) before the child has done anything.

faq.q: Isn't it dangerous to tell people to see the image of God in their enemy or their abuser?
faq.a: It would be dangerous to teach it carelessly, and the study works hard not to. Seeing the image in someone doesn't mean trusting them, staying within their reach, or failing to protect yourself and others from them. Where there's abuse, the faithful thing is safety, distance and real help; the help information with this guide is there for that. Seeing the image means refusing to let even a dangerous person become less than human in your eyes, which keeps the fight against evil from turning you into it.

faq.q: What does the study say about the worth of people with severe disabilities or dementia?
faq.a: Their worth is exactly as full as anyone's, and this is one of the places the doctrine matters most. If the image were grounded in a capacity like reason, people with severe disabilities or dementia would seem to have less of it. But the image is first a status God gives, a calling he issues and a relationship he establishes, and none of those depends on what a person can do. A relationship can hold someone who can't respond.

faq.q: How does the image of God relate to Jesus? Why bring Christ into a doctrine from Genesis?
faq.a: Because the doctrine was never meant to end in Genesis. Genesis says Adam was made in the image. The New Testament says Christ is "the image of the invisible God" (Colossians 1:15). Humanity was patterned after the Son from the beginning, and salvation is being "conformed to the image of his Son" (Romans 8:29). The image was defaced in a garden and is restored in a person.

faq.q: I'm a skeptic. Isn't the image of God just a comforting story we tell to feel special?
faq.a: It's a fair suspicion, and the study takes it seriously. It grants freely that humans are creatures made of dust and kin to the animals, as Genesis itself says. But it asks whether the reduction can explain how all of us actually live: outraged by cruelty, grieved at gravesides, sure that a child matters more than a stone. You can't get boundless human worth out of atoms and appetite. The image is offered as the explanation of a dignity everyone already assumes. You don't have to believe it to notice that your moral life is written in its language.

faq.q: How do I lead this if I know I struggle to see the image in certain people?
faq.a: That struggle doesn't disqualify you; it's what the study runs on. This isn't a study for someone who has arrived at perfect sight. Name your own hard cases early and plainly, go first on the self-implicating questions, and let the room see a leader still learning to see. A leader who pretends to see every face rightly teaches the room to pretend too.

faq.q: Does taking the image this seriously mean I have to agree with everyone or approve of everything people do?
faq.a: No. Seeing the image in a person isn't trusting them, approving of them or agreeing with them. You can disagree sharply, name wrong plainly, hold someone accountable and protect others from them, and still refuse to treat them as less than human. The image doesn't lower the bar on behavior. It raises the bar on contempt.

timeline.event: Genesis 1 declares that God made humanity, male and female, in his own image and likeness, taking a title the surrounding empires reserved for the king alone and handing it to every human being, the most radical claim about human worth in the ancient world.

Genesis 3 narrates the defacing of the image, the creature made to represent God grasping instead to be God, fracturing the reason, the will, and the relationships the image was made to hold, so that the likeness is marred but, as later chapters show, never erased.

Genesis 9 grounds the sanctity of human life in the image, spoken over sinful survivors, proving that the fall did not destroy the likeness, since the protection of every remaining human life rests on an image that fallen people still bear.
Psalm 8, attributed to David, sings the paradox of the image: a creature of dust made "a little lower than the heavenly beings" and "crowned... with glory and honor" (Psalm 8:5).
Jesus of Nazareth lives as the image of God in human flesh, so that "whoever has seen me has seen the Father" (John 14:9).
Paul's letters call Christ "the image of the invisible God" (Colossians 1:15) and describe salvation as believers being "conformed to the image of his Son" (Romans 8:29).
Augustine, especially in On the Trinity, finds the image in the soul's memory, understanding and will, shaping the substantive reading that dominated Christian thought for more than a thousand years.
Thomas Aquinas, in the Summa Theologiae, grounds the image in the intellect, the rational nature that distinguishes humans from animals, giving the substantive view its classic medieval form.

John Calvin, in the editions of his Institutes, teaches that the fall didn't wholly destroy the image but corrupted it into a frightful deformity, restored only in Christ. Later Reformed theologians build on this with the language of a broad and a narrow image.

Dietrich Bonhoeffer lectures on Genesis in Berlin, published as Creation and Fall, describing the image as a relation God establishes and as freedom for the other, as the regime that would later execute him comes to power.
Karl Barth, in Church Dogmatics III/1, develops the relational reading, finding the image in human beings made for relationship, male and female, answering to the relationship God himself is.
J. Richard Middleton publishes The Liberating Image, arguing in detail that Genesis 1 gives the royal image to all humanity against the ideology of the ancient empires.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome, and thank you for being here. It takes some courage to look at what a human being is worth and why. Before we start, three things. First, this isn't a study about human dignity in general, which is easy to affirm and costs nothing. It's about whether we can see the image of God in the specific people we'd rather not, and the only sight any of us is responsible for here is our own. Second, this doctrine belongs to no political side, and we're going to let it cut against every tribe, including our own, so come ready to hear your own side's blind spot named as plainly as your opponents'. Third, none of us sees perfectly. I'm not teaching the rest of you to catch up; we're all still learning to see. One more thing, and I mean it. If anything tonight comes near a real wound you carry, a loss, a crisis, an abuser, you don't have to perform anything. I'm available to talk privately and to help you find help. Tonight we're looking at this together: ________. I'll read our key passage, and then we'll sit with it before anyone says anything. There are no wrong answers in the first five minutes.
facilitatorScript.transition: We've looked hard at what this session says. Now let's bring it off the page and into the week each of us walked in from and will walk back into, real faces and real encounters, because a doctrine of the image that changes nothing on Monday was never believed on Sunday.
facilitatorScript.close: We're going to stop there, even though it doesn't resolve. This doctrine convicts and then sends you out still carrying it. Take the weight home rather than leaving it at the door. Try the practice this week with a real person, even if you do it badly. Sit with the reflection questions on your own, and come back ready to be honest, not finished. I'll pray for us before we go. Remember, there are no ordinary people. And my door is open if any of you needs it.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, set the ground rules about seeing your own blind spot and refusing the tribal capture of the doctrine, and walk session one's opening questions slowly.
Week 2: Session 1, The Image the Kings Kept for Themselves, with extra time on the ancient background and the democratization of the image.
Week 3: Session 2, What the Image Is, part one, the three views laid out and the danger of grounding worth in a capacity.
Week 4: Session 2 continued, the order that holds the three views together and the pastoral payoff for the disabled and the weak, with care for anyone it touches closely.
Week 5: Session 3, Defaced but Not Destroyed, holding the seriousness of sin and the surviving dignity together.
Week 6: Session 4, The True Image, and the One We Are Becoming, formation as restoration by beholding rather than self-improvement by striving.
Week 7: Session 5, The Image in the Street, walking the list of the poor, the unborn, the enemy, the stranger, and the person who annoys you, with the tribal trap named in both directions.
Week 8: Integration. Revisit all five practices, the scripture index, and whose face each person is going home to finally see, closing in the God who assigns a worth we cannot revoke.

cadences.name: The intensive (4 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Sessions 1 and 2 together, the image taken out of the palace and the argument over what it is and why it decides who counts as fully human.
Week 2: Session 3, Defaced but Not Destroyed, the image marred by the fall and never erased.
Week 3: Session 4, The True Image, and the One We Are Becoming, Christ the image and the restoration of the ruined likeness.
Week 4: Session 5, The Image in the Street, plus a short integration close in the dignity that stands over every tribe and belongs to none.

bibliography.note: Bonhoeffer's Berlin lectures of 1932 to 1933, published in 1933, describing the image as a relation God establishes and as freedom for God and for others. Background for sessions 2, 3 and 5.

bibliography.title: Church Dogmatics, III/1 and III/2
bibliography.author: Karl Barth
bibliography.note: Barth's development of the relational reading (III/1 appeared in German in 1945), in which human beings, made for relationship, answer to the relationship God himself is. Dense; for the leader who wants the source of the relational view in session 2.

bibliography.title: Mere Christianity
bibliography.author: C. S. Lewis
bibliography.note: General background on the moral argument, useful for the skeptic's objection in session 1 that human worth can't be built from below. The line about there being no ordinary people comes from "The Weight of Glory," not this book.

bibliography.title: The Weight of Glory
bibliography.author: C. S. Lewis
bibliography.note: Lewis's 1941 sermon, later collected in The Weight of Glory and Other Addresses (1949), with the passage about there being no ordinary people quoted in session 5.

bibliography.title: Institutes of the Christian Religion
bibliography.author: John Calvin
bibliography.note: Calvin's teaching that the fall corrupted but didn't wholly destroy the image (Book 1, chapter 15). The historical anchor for session 3. First published in 1536; the final edition is 1559.

bibliography.title: Dignity and Destiny: Humanity in the Image of God
bibliography.author: John F. Kilner
bibliography.note: Published in 2015. A thorough evangelical study of the image that grounds human dignity in what God gives rather than in human capacities, close to this study's insistence on the order. Supports sessions 2 and 3.

bibliography.title: Bonhoeffer: Pastor, Martyr, Prophet, Spy
bibliography.author: Eric Metaxas
bibliography.note: Published in 2010. A popular biography that gives the setting of Bonhoeffer's resistance. Some historians have criticized it, so read it alongside Bonhoeffer's own writings.

bibliography.title: The Book of Genesis, Chapters 1-17 (New International Commentary)
bibliography.author: Victor P. Hamilton
bibliography.note: Published in 1990. A standard evangelical commentary on the creation and fall texts, for leaders who want verse-by-verse grounding for sessions 1 and 3.

bibliography.title: Genesis
bibliography.author: the book of Genesis
bibliography.note: The primary text beneath the whole study, especially chapters 1, 3, 5 and 9, where the image is made, defaced, passed on and protected.

furtherReading: The Liberating Image, J. Richard Middleton, for the full scholarly case that Genesis 1 gives the royal image to everyone, behind sessions 1 and 5.
Creation and Fall, Dietrich Bonhoeffer, for the relational reading of the image from a man who resisted a regime built on ranking human lives.
The Weight of Glory, C. S. Lewis, especially its closing pages on there being no ordinary people, the heart of session 5 in a single sermon.
Dignity and Destiny, John F. Kilner, for a thorough case that human worth rests on what God gives rather than on our capacities, supporting sessions 2 and 3.
Genesis 1 through 9, read straight through, to watch the image made, defaced, passed on and protected before reading any commentary.

glossary.definition: The Latin phrase for the image of God, the biblical teaching that human beings are made in God's image and likeness, given a dignity and a vocation no other creature has. The subject of the whole study, drawn from Genesis 1:26-27.

The Hebrew word translated image in Genesis 1, ordinarily used for a statue set up to represent a god in a temple. It casts the human being as God's statue placed in the temple of his creation, made to represent him and show what he is like.

The Hebrew word translated likeness in Genesis 1, paired with tselem. Most interpreters read the two as a poetic parallelism naming a single reality rather than two separate things, guarding against building large doctrines on a small grammatical difference.

The recognition that Genesis takes the divine image, reserved in the surrounding empires for the king alone, and extends it to every human being, male and female, slave and free, the liberation J. Richard Middleton names in The Liberating Image.

The classic reading, running from Augustine and Aquinas through most of the tradition, that the image is a quality inside us, most often reason or the rational soul. It honors what is distinctive in humans but risks grounding worth in a capacity some possess less of.

The reading, closest to Genesis in its ancient context, that the image is a vocation, the calling to represent God and steward his creation as his royal representatives. It protects the worth of those who cannot exercise the role, since a vocation can be conferred and held in trust.

The reading, developed by Barth and Bonhoeffer, that the image is found in the relationships we stand in, with God and with one another. It protects the worth of those who cannot respond, since a relationship God establishes holds a person even when every capacity fails.

The two-sided truth about the fall's effect on the image, that sin marred it grievously in every part yet never erased it, so that fallen human beings still bear the image, which is why no person is ever beyond worth or beyond hope.

A distinction used by Reformed theologians after Calvin: the broad image is the human constitution that survives the fall (reason, conscience, relationship, the calling to rule); the narrow image is the original righteousness, knowledge and holiness lost in the fall and restored in Christ.

Jesus Christ, whom Paul calls the image of the invisible God, not a bearer of the image but the image itself, the true original of which Adam and all humanity are copies, and the pattern into which the defaced image is being remade.

The New Testament description of salvation as the defaced image being restored into the likeness of Christ, changed from one degree of glory to another by beholding him, so that Christian formation is the ruined humanity being made truly human at last.

The biblical principle that we are formed into the image of whatever holds our gaze and worship, so that the Christian is changed by beholding Christ, and, on the sobering flip side, deformed into the image of any idol we fix our eyes on instead.

The failure of turning the image of God into a weapon for one political side, wielded to defend the people a tribe already favors and to indict only its opponents, which empties the doctrine, since a true doctrine of the image cuts against every tribe with the same blade.

The conviction, put memorably by C. S. Lewis, that because every human bears the image, there are no ordinary or disposable people and no face safe to despise, so that how we treat any person is how we treat their Maker.

promoKit.bulletinBlurb: The Bible's oldest and boldest claim about people is that they're made in the image of God, and few of us stop to ask what that means or how it should change the way we treat anyone. This five-session study starts with a sentence in Genesis that sounded closer to sedition than compliment in its own world, works through the argument over what the image is, faces the fall that defaced it without erasing it, turns to Christ, the true image, who restores it, and ends in the street, where the poor, the unborn, the enemy, the stranger and the person who annoys you all carry a worth we didn't assign and can't revoke. It belongs to no political side. Any group can lead it with no prep. Come honest, not finished.
promoKit.pulpitAnnouncement: We're starting a five-week study on the image of God, and it isn't the abstract, agreeable thing the phrase might suggest. It takes the oldest claim the Bible makes about human worth and follows it into how we actually treat people: the poor, the unborn, the enemy, the stranger and the one who simply annoys us. It won't be captured by any political side; it lets the doctrine cut against every tribe, including our own. It faces the fall and lands on Christ, the true image, who makes us human at last. No homework, and no prep needed to lead a group. Sign up at the welcome table.
promoKit.inviteCaption: The Bible's boldest claim about people is that every one of them bears the image of God. This five-session study takes that claim into the street: what the image is, the fall that defaced it, Christ who restores it, and the faces we'd rather not see it in. It belongs to no political side. Come honest, not finished.
quoteCards: The empires around Israel kept the divine image in the palace. Genesis gave it to everyone.
The argument about what the image is turns out to be the argument about who gets counted as fully human.
A defaced image is still an image. The signature is still under the ruin.
Being saved isn't becoming something other than human. It's becoming human at last.
We're changed into his likeness not by straining at the mirror but by looking at him.
If a doctrine only ever convicts the other side, it has become a tribe in robes.
A gift can't be graded, and no one falls below the line.
How you treat the image is how you treat the one it images.
